segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: An interesting thing about prepositions is that they have a habit of changing between languages.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: To give you an example, in English we say "I fall in love with".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: In Spanish, you say "I enamor myself of"—"I fall in love of you".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now again, this is something that we look at with interest rather than looking at it as an obstacle, for the insight that it might give us about how we perceive and express the world through our own language.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, the fact that we use "with" is not necessarily casual—casual in the sense of meaningless.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The fact that we use "with" is not necessarily without its weight, without its meaning. If I say "I fall in love with you",

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: that preposition "with" necessarily involves you in my process of falling in love.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, this "of" is much more detached in feeling than "with".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So there is a school of thought which explores how these elements of language might have a real, tangible effect on the way we interact with the world, and with certain concepts, and the way we express them, and how that feeds back into the way we perceive and view the world.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And I think this is a very nice example between falling in love with and falling in love of.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So this is something to think about and just take interest in whenever you find that in Spanish the verb uses a different preposition than the one it does in English, rather than just seeing it as a hurdle to correctness that you need to memorize, maybe have a little look at how it might actually be affecting, somehow or other, the way you perceive the world.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: This also helps the memory on a practical level. You are much more capable of internalizing and remembering this difference if rather than just mindlessly memorizing that you're using de instead of con here,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: we are looking with a more analytical eye, with a curious eye, to understand what effect this might possibly have on us. And in this way, we're just going to learn the differences much easier.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Let's start with this verb. To fall in love is to enamor oneself. So if you look up in the dictionary "to fall in love",

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: what you will find is enamorarse, written as one word. Now, it's important to realize that it's not one word. You still have a verb there ending -ar, enamorar, and then the se is just hooked on. So let's start with "I fall in love".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How will you make enamorarse "I fall in love" / "I enamor myself"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Me enamoro.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Exactly. Me enamoro.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now if you want to say "I fall in love with you"—we're probably going to speak informally—in Spanish, we're not going to say "with you", we're going to say "of you": "I enamor myself of you".

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Me enamoro de ti.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yeah. Me enamoro de ti. Very good. "I fall in love with him"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Me enamoro de él.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Me enamoro de él. If we want to give the meaning of "I am falling in love right now", we can say "I am"—how is "I am" from estar?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estoy.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "Falling in love" / "enamoring myself"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Enamorando... me.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. It can come actually after the -ando or before estoy: Estoy enamorándome, me estoy enamorando de él.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Another verb that uses a different preposition in Spanish and English is the verb "to think".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "To think", we said it was related to the word "pensive", which means "thoughtful".

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Pensar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Pensar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, you don't say "I think about you" in Spanish, you say "I'm thinking" or "I think in" or "on you". What was the word for "in" and "on"? I think we looked at it very briefly.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: En.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: En. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we say "I think in you" or "on you". It's probably "in", actually, because Arabic says it in this way, and of course, when languages come into contact,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: like the 800 years of contact that Spanish and Arabic had, they share a lot more than vocabulary, they also share structures.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we're probably saying "I'm thinking in you" to say "I think about you". So how do you say that, "I'm thinking about you" or "I think about you"? Let's keep it informal.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Penso... sorry, pienso en ti.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Pienso en ti. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say "we think about you" or "we're thinking about you"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Pensamos en ti.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Pensamos en ti. "We think about her", or "we think in her", or literally "we think in she"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Pensamos en ella.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Pensamos en ella. To dream in Spanish is soñar.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Soñar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: This "ny" sound like the one we have in mañana is with the eñe. Eñe is the only letter that we get in Spanish that we don't get in English, and it's like an n with a little squiggly line on the top of the n, and it's basically n-y.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So n with squiggly line on top is n-y like in mañana, like in soñar. Soñar: to dream.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Soñar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How do you think you say "I dream"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Soño.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Would be soño, but what might happen? How is "to sleep"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Dormir.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Dormir. And "I sleep"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Duermo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Mm.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Sueño?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yeah. So this is happening here, but there's really no way to know if it's going to happen or not. Sometimes it does, sometimes it doesn't, huh? If it happens for one of the versions, of course it's going to happen for all of the versions that we stress the o, so sueño, sueña, sueñan, sueñas.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But "we dream"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Soñamos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Soñamos, because we're not stressing it anymore. Soñamos, we're stressing the a. Very good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We don't say "I dream of" in Spanish, we say "I dream with". So here we use "with" in Spanish: "I dream with her".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The language, we said, is permitting and requiring us to perceive and express the world in a certain way.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So when we say, you know, "I dream with her", maybe you can imagine that when people began to talk about what they were dreaming, that they had the idea of the involvement of the other person, you know, "I'm dreaming with you".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Well, you don't know, but it's interesting to think about how that change in the preposition can really affect the way we perceive the world, and then subconsciously, because even though our beliefs might have modernized,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: like if I dream about you, I don't really think you're there and I don't really think you're participating, huh? But the language might hold an old belief that it is with you, that you are actually participating in my dream.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So it's interesting to think about, and thinking about it is going to help your memory internalize just this simple fact that the preposition changes.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say "I dream about her", or in Spanish "I dream" or "I'm dreaming with her"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Sueño con ella.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Sueño con ella. Good. "He dreams about him"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Sueña con él.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Sueña con él. Good. What was "for me"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Para mí.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And "for you", informal?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Para ti.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And what was "from"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: De.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: De. "From me"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: De mí.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "From you", informal?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: De ti.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: De ti. Good. With "with", we get a little exception. "With me" is conmigo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And it's spelled like one word. So this -go is coming from nowhere, and it's all becoming one word, where de mí, para mí are two separate words. So we have conmigo for "with me", and contigo, "with you", informal.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Conmigo: c-o-n-m-i-g-o. Or contigo: c-o-n-t-i-g-o. So this is "with me", "with you". What was "to come"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Venir.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Venir: to come. Good. So how would you say, speaking informally, "do you want to come with me"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿Quieres venir conmigo?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "Don't you want to come with me"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿No quieres venir conmigo?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No quieres venir conmigo. "Why don't you want to come with me"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿Por qué no quieres venir conmigo?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. ¿Por qué no quieres venir conmigo? What was "I have" in the sense of possession?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Tengo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tengo. Good. And if we want to say "I have to", we can add something to that tengo, and it's not a comfortable translation either, if that helps you remember it.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Tengo que.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tengo que. Good. So how would you say "you have to come with me"? Again, speaking informally, "you have to come with me".

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Tienes que venir conmigo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tienes que venir conmigo. Good. Good. What was "I can", from "to be able"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Puedo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Puedo. "Can you come with me", still informal?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿Puedes venir conmigo?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Puedes venir conmigo. So we have conmigo for "with me", contigo for "with you" speaking informally. So we could say "I dream about you",

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: and we're going to say "I dream with you", speaking informally.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Sueño contigo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Sueño contigo. "I'm going with you", informally still.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: I'm going... I'm forgetting the verbs.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: You will forget them many times. And you need to find the way that you dig them up. That's the most important thing, to take this skill away. So going, what does going relate to, if anything?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ah, voyage. Voy.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: You see? "I'm going with you", speaking informally?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Voy contigo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. "To depend" in Spanish is depender. Depender. How would you say "it depends"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Dependa.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Make sure before you start to change any verb you do the quick check to see what type of verb it is.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Depende.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes. Depender, -er verb, depende. Good. Now, in Spanish we don't say "it depends on", we say "it depends of".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say "it depends on her" or "it depends of her"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Depende de ella.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Depende de ella. The word for "yes" and the word for "if" are the same in Spanish. So, you know how to say "yes" in Spanish?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Sí.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Sí. Good. So this is also "if". "It depends on if she wants to go". Let's say that: "It depends"...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Depende...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ...on or it depends of in Spanish...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ...good, "if she wants to go"...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ...si quiere ir.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So all together: "It depends on if she wants to go"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Depende de si quiere ir.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Depende de si quiere ir. It depends on if she wants to go.
